title: Content-Based Filtering
summary: Recommend from item features and a user's own history alone — no other users' data required, and no filter-bubble-free lunch either.

slides.markdown:
Content-based filtering represents every item as a **feature vector** — structured attributes (genre, price, brand), tags, or a text/image embedding of its description. A movie might be `[genre: sci-fi, director: Nolan, runtime: 148, embedding: ...]`.

Once items live in a shared feature space, "similar item" becomes a geometric question: compute a distance or cosine similarity between vectors. This is the whole trick — recommendation reduces to nearest-neighbor search over item vectors, which is why it's often the simplest recommender to ship first.

To recommend for a user, build a **user profile vector** — typically the average (or weighted average, favoring recent activity) of the feature vectors of items they've liked. Then rank all candidate items by similarity to that profile.

Liked three dark psychological thrillers in a row? The profile vector sits in "thriller" space, so the next recommendation is another thriller — no other user's data was ever consulted. This is entirely self-contained per user, which is both the strength (works with zero other users) and the limitation (never learns from anyone else's taste).

For text-heavy items (articles, product descriptions, job listings), the feature vector is usually **TF-IDF** or a learned **embedding** (from a model like word2vec or a sentence transformer). Cosine similarity between two TF-IDF or embedding vectors stands in for "how similar are these two pieces of text."

Embeddings generally beat TF-IDF for this because they capture meaning, not just shared words — "laptop" and "notebook computer" land close together in embedding space even with zero overlapping tokens.

Pure content-based filtering **over-narrows**. Because it only ever recommends things similar to what you already liked, it has no mechanism for surfacing anything genuinely new — you liked thrillers, so you get thrillers forever, and the catalog's romance and documentary sections might as well not exist for you.

This is the classic **filter bubble**: recommendations that are locally accurate but globally boring, with zero serendipity. There's no cross-user signal at all to say "people like you, who also loved thrillers, unexpectedly loved this one documentary" — that leap requires collaborative signal, which content-based filtering structurally can't provide.

| | Content-based | Collaborative filtering |
|---|---|---|
| Needs other users? | No | Yes |
| New-item cold start | Solved (uses item's own features) | Broken (no interactions yet) |
| New-user cold start | Still broken (needs the user's own history) | Still broken |
| Serendipity | Low (filter bubble) | Higher (cross-user patterns) |

**How to decide:** content-based filtering solves new-item cold start but not new-user cold start — it needs *a* history to work from, just not anyone else's. That's exactly the gap collaborative filtering fills, which is why production systems combine both rather than picking one.

slides.subTitle: Computing cosine similarity by hand
slides.markdown:
Say a user's profile vector is `[0.8, 0.6]` (high action, medium comedy) and a candidate item is `[0.6, 0.8]` (medium action, high comedy). **Cosine similarity** measures the angle between them, ignoring magnitude: `dot product / (|vector1| * |vector2|)`.

The dot product is `0.8*0.6 + 0.6*0.8 = 0.48 + 0.48 = 0.96`. Each vector's magnitude is `sqrt(0.8² + 0.6²) = 1.0` (both happen to already be unit vectors here), so cosine similarity is `0.96 / (1.0 * 1.0) = 0.96` — very high, correctly reflecting that these two vectors point in a similar direction even though neither dimension matches exactly. This is the exact computation behind every "similar item" ranking in a content-based system.

slides.subTitle: Explicit diversity injection
slides.markdown:
Since content-based filtering structurally can't inject cross-user serendipity, production systems that rely heavily on it fight the filter bubble with explicit rules rather than a smarter similarity function: reserve a small slot quota for items outside the user's dominant profile cluster, occasionally rank by a *secondary* feature dimension instead of overall similarity (surface a well-reviewed documentary even to a thriller-heavy profile), or deliberately decay the weight of very old liked items in the profile so a single early binge doesn't permanently pin the user's taste.

These are the same re-ranking pattern seen in [ranking-hybrid-recommenders](ranking-hybrid-recommenders) — a deterministic post-processing layer bolted onto the similarity score, rather than something the core content-based algorithm can fix on its own.

slides.subTitle: One-hot categorical features vs learned embeddings
slides.markdown:
Building an item's feature vector requires a choice for each attribute. **One-hot encoding** a categorical field (genre, brand) gives each value its own dimension — simple and exact, but every value is equally "far" from every other (comedy is just as different from drama as it is from documentary, which isn't quite true).

**Learned embeddings** for categorical fields (train a small embedding table jointly with the rest of the model, or borrow one from a related task) let related categories land closer together — comedy and romantic-comedy can end up nearer each other than comedy and horror, capturing structure one-hot encoding can't represent at all. The trade-off is the usual one: one-hot is simpler and needs no training, embeddings need enough data per category to learn a meaningful position.

slides.subTitle: Stale item features silently degrade recommendations
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Once we've computed an item's feature vector, it stays valid indefinitely."

**Why it's wrong:** item metadata changes — a product's category gets recategorized, an article gets updated tags, a movie's crowd-sourced genre tags shift as more people rate it. If the feature vector is computed once at ingestion and never refreshed, the similarity computation is silently working off **outdated** information indefinitely, and nothing in the system surfaces this as an error — recommendations just quietly get a little worse over time with no obvious failure signal.

**Correct model:** treat item feature vectors as a **living artifact** that needs a refresh pipeline (recompute embeddings when metadata changes, or on a regular schedule), the same way a feature store needs a refresh strategy for any other input — not a one-time batch job you run once at launch and forget.
